prompts.L1:
Please polish the following text to make it more eloquent and professional, keeping all original information unchanged:

We observe a sharp transition from a singular, high-mass mode of star formation, to a low-mass dominated mode, in numerical simulations, at a metallicity of 10^-3 Zsolar. We incorporate a new method for including the radiative cooling from metals into adaptive mesh-refinement hydrodynamic simulations. Our results illustrate how metals, produced by the first stars, led to a transition from the high-mass star formation mode of Pop III stars, to the low-mass mode that dominates today. We ran hydrodynamic simulations with cosmological initial conditions in the standard LambdaCDM model, with metallicities, from zero to 10^-2 Zsolar, beginnning at redshift, z = 99. The simulations were run until a dense core forms at the center of a 5 x 10^5 Msolar dark matter halo, at z ~ 18. Analysis of the central 1 Msolar core reveals that the two simulations with the lowest metallicities, Z = 0 and 10^-4 Zsolar, contain one clump with 99% of the mass, while the two with metallicities, Z = 10^-3 and 10^-2 Zsolar, each contain two clumps that share most of the mass. The Z = 10^-3 Zsolar simulation also produced two low-mass proto-stellar objects with masses between 10^-2 and 10^-1 Msolar. Gas with Z >= 10^-3 Zsolar is able to cool to the temperature of the CMB, which sets a lower limit to the minimum fragmentation mass. This suggests that the second generation stars produced a spectrum of lower mass stars, but were still more massive on average than stars formed in the local universe.

outputs.L1:
We observe a sharp transition in numerical simulations from a single, high-mass mode of star formation to a low-mass-dominated mode at a metallicity of \(10^{-3}\,Z_{\odot}\). We introduce a new method for incorporating radiative cooling by metals into adaptive mesh-refinement hydrodynamic simulations. Our results illustrate how metals produced by the first stars drove the transition from the high-mass star formation mode characteristic of Population III stars to the low-mass mode that dominates today.

We performed hydrodynamic simulations with cosmological initial conditions in the standard \(\Lambda\)CDM model, adopting metallicities ranging from zero to \(10^{-2}\,Z_{\odot}\) and beginning at redshift \(z=99\). Each simulation was evolved until a dense core formed at the center of a \(5 \times 10^{5}\,M_{\odot}\) dark matter halo at \(z \sim 18\). Analysis of the central \(1\,M_{\odot}\) core reveals that the two lowest-metallicity simulations, with \(Z=0\) and \(10^{-4}\,Z_{\odot}\), each contain a single clump comprising 99% of the mass. By contrast, the simulations with \(Z=10^{-3}\) and \(10^{-2}\,Z_{\odot}\) each contain two clumps that share most of the mass. The \(Z=10^{-3}\,Z_{\odot}\) simulation also produced two low-mass protostellar objects with masses between \(10^{-2}\) and \(10^{-1}\,M_{\odot}\).

Gas with \(Z \geq 10^{-3}\,Z_{\odot}\) can cool to the temperature of the cosmic microwave background, which imposes a lower limit on the minimum fragmentation mass. These findings suggest that second-generation stars formed with a spectrum extending to lower masses, although their average masses remained higher than those of stars formed in the local universe.
outputs.L2:
Our numerical simulations identify an abrupt shift in star formation at a metallicity of \(10^{-3}\,Z_{\odot}\), changing from a mode characterized by a single massive object to one dominated by lower-mass objects. To model this process, we developed a new approach for incorporating metal-line radiative cooling into adaptive mesh-refinement hydrodynamic calculations.

The simulations used cosmological initial conditions based on the standard \(\Lambda\)CDM model. They began at redshift \(z=99\) and covered metallicities ranging from zero to \(10^{-2}\,Z_{\odot}\). Each run continued until a dense central core developed within a \(5\times10^{5}\,M_{\odot}\) dark matter halo at approximately \(z=18\).

An examination of the innermost \(1\,M_{\odot}\) core shows a clear metallicity-dependent difference. In the two lowest-metallicity cases, \(Z=0\) and \(Z=10^{-4}\,Z_{\odot}\), a single clump contains 99% of the mass. By contrast, the \(Z=10^{-3}\,Z_{\odot}\) and \(Z=10^{-2}\,Z_{\odot}\) simulations each form two clumps that together account for most of the mass. The \(Z=10^{-3}\,Z_{\odot}\) run also creates two low-mass protostellar objects with masses between \(10^{-2}\) and \(10^{-1}\,M_{\odot}\).

At metallicities of \(Z\geq10^{-3}\,Z_{\odot}\), the gas can cool to the cosmic microwave background temperature, which imposes a lower bound on the minimum fragmentation mass. These findings demonstrate how metals synthesized by the first stars could have driven the transition from the massive Population III star-formation regime to the low-mass-dominated mode seen today. They further indicate that second-generation stars formed with a range of lower masses, although their average mass likely remained greater than that of stars forming in the present-day local universe.
outputs.L3:
Numerical simulations reveal a sharp transition from high-mass to low-mass-dominated star formation at a critical metallicity of approximately \(10^{-3}\,Z_\odot\). These simulations included metal-line radiative cooling and examined gas with metallicities ranging from zero to \(10^{-2}\,Z_\odot\) within a \(5 \times 10^{5}\,M_\odot\) dark matter halo.

At zero metallicity and at \(10^{-4}\,Z_\odot\), fragmentation was limited: a single clump contained 99% of the mass in the central core. By contrast, simulations at higher metallicities produced two dominant clumps, indicating that metal enrichment substantially increased the tendency of the gas to fragment. Notably, the simulation at \(10^{-3}\,Z_\odot\) also formed two low-mass protostellar objects with masses between \(10^{-2}\) and \(10^{-1}\,M_\odot\).

The underlying cause of this transition is the greater cooling efficiency of metal-enriched gas. At metallicities of \(10^{-3}\,Z_\odot\) or higher, metal-line emission allows the gas to cool to the temperature of the cosmic microwave background. This lower temperature promotes fragmentation and supports the formation of lower-mass, second-generation stars. Although these stars were less massive than the first, metal-free stars, their average masses were still expected to exceed those of stars forming in the present-day Universe.
outputs.L4:
The first stars, known as Population III stars, formed from nearly pristine hydrogen and helium and were probably much more massive than most stars born today. Their radiation, winds, and supernova explosions enriched the surrounding medium with heavy elements, enabling gas to cool more efficiently and opening the way for subsequent generations of stars. To investigate how this chemical enrichment changed the characteristic pattern of star formation, cosmological adaptive-mesh hydrodynamic simulations followed the collapse of gas in dark-matter halos while including radiative cooling from metal emission lines. The calculations considered metallicities ranging from completely metal-free gas to \(10^{-2}\,Z_\odot\), where \(Z_\odot\) is the solar metallicity.

At the lowest metallicities, cooling remained inefficient, and the collapsing gas behaved much like primordial material. It stayed comparatively warm, developed relatively little small-scale structure, and tended to form only one or a few massive protostellar condensations. Increasing the abundance of heavy elements strengthened radiative cooling, but the effect was not gradual across the full metallicity range. Instead, the simulations revealed a pronounced transition at a metallicity of roughly \(10^{-3}\,Z_\odot\).

Above this threshold, metal-line emission allowed the gas to cool rapidly until it reached the temperature of the cosmic microwave background. Because the CMB sets a redshift-dependent minimum temperature, further radiative cooling could not substantially lower the gas temperature. Nevertheless, reaching this floor reduced the thermal pressure enough for the cloud to become strongly gravitationally unstable. The collapsing material broke into several dense clumps, producing multiple protostellar objects rather than a single dominant massive star. Some of these fragments had relatively low initial masses and could potentially have evolved into long-lived, low-mass stars, although later accretion and dynamical interactions would still influence their final masses.

The results therefore support the existence of a critical metallicity associated with the transition from Population III star formation to a more fragmented mode characteristic of chemically enriched gas. This transition should not be interpreted as an immediate shift to the modern stellar initial mass function. At the high redshifts studied, the elevated CMB temperature imposed a cooling floor that kept the characteristic fragmentation mass above that found in present-day molecular clouds. Consequently, the first metal-enriched, or second-generation, stars were likely drawn from a broader mass distribution than Population III stars and included substantially lower-mass objects, while still being more massive on average than stars forming in the contemporary Universe.

These findings show that even modest enrichment—about one-thousandth of the Sun’s metallicity—could fundamentally alter the thermal evolution and fragmentation of primordial star-forming clouds. They also emphasize that metallicity alone did not determine stellar masses: the CMB temperature, collapse environment, accretion history, and subsequent interactions among protostars all helped shape the final stellar population.
outputs.L5:
### Zsolar: Powering Our Pop Culture with Clean Energy

Zsolar brings renewable energy into the heart of our everyday lives. From outdoor concerts and pop-up events to homes and creative spaces, solar power offers a cleaner way to keep the music playing and communities connected. By choosing Zsolar, we can support our planet while building a brighter, more sustainable pop culture for the future.

counterfactuals.prompt: Summarize the results of a study on the critical metallicity for the transition from Population III star formation to low-mass star formation in early dark matter halos.
counterfactuals.output:
The study found that the transition from massive Population III star formation to lower-mass, Population II-like star formation is not set by one universal metallicity.

- **Metal-free gas** cools mainly through molecular hydrogen, typically reaching a temperature floor of about 200 K and fragmenting into relatively massive clumps.
- **Metal-line cooling**, especially from carbon and oxygen, becomes effective at a metallicity of roughly  
  \[
  Z_{\rm crit}\sim10^{-4}-10^{-3}\,Z_\odot
  \]
  often quoted as \(10^{-3.5}Z_\odot\). This promotes greater fragmentation, although it does not always produce solar-mass stars.
- If **dust grains** are present, cooling at much higher densities can trigger very small-scale fragmentation at metallicities as low as  
  \[
  Z_{\rm crit}\sim10^{-6}-10^{-5}\,Z_\odot.
  \]

Thus, the key conclusion is that the “critical metallicity” depends strongly on the dust abundance, carbon and oxygen enrichment, gas density, radiation field, and collapse history of the dark-matter halo. Dust cooling provides the most plausible route to forming long-lived, sub-solar-mass stars at the extremely low metallicities observed in some ancient Galactic stars.
counterfactuals.label: cf_1

counterfactuals.prompt: Write an abstract describing cosmological adaptive mesh-refinement simulations of metal-enriched star formation, including the metallicity range, halo properties, fragmentation behavior, and the role of the CMB temperature floor.
counterfactuals.output: We present three-dimensional cosmological adaptive mesh-refinement simulations of metal-enriched star formation in primordial halos, following gravitational collapse from cosmological initial conditions to sub-parsec scales. The calculations span metallicities \(Z=10^{-6}\)–\(10^{-2}\,Z_\odot\) in halos with virial masses of approximately \(10^{6}\)–\(10^{8}\,M_\odot\) collapsing at redshifts \(z\sim10\)–25. At the lowest metallicities, cooling remains dominated by primordial species, producing warm, centrally concentrated collapse with limited fragmentation. Above a critical abundance of roughly \(10^{-4}\)–\(10^{-3}\,Z_\odot\), metal-line cooling lowers the gas temperature, promotes the formation of filaments and dense clumps, and substantially increases fragmentation. This trend is not monotonic, however: once enriched gas cools to the cosmic microwave background (CMB) temperature, further cooling is prevented. The resulting nearly isothermal phase is followed by reheating at higher density, increasing the characteristic Jeans mass and reducing fragmentation relative to calculations without a radiation-temperature floor. Our results show that early stellar multiplicity and characteristic fragment masses depend jointly on metallicity, halo assembly history, and redshift, with the CMB establishing a redshift-dependent minimum temperature that can favor comparatively massive stars even in strongly enriched gas.
counterfactuals.label: cf_2

counterfactuals.prompt: At what metallicity do numerical simulations predict a transition from high-mass Population III stars to lower-mass second-generation stars? Explain the simulation setup and key findings.
counterfactuals.output:
Numerical simulations generally place the **critical metallicity** for the transition at

\[
Z_{\rm crit}\sim10^{-3.5}Z_\odot,
\]

i.e. a few \(10^{-4}\) of the solar metallicity. In many early calculations the transition appeared between \(10^{-4}\) and \(10^{-3}Z_\odot\), so it is often quoted as \(Z_{\rm crit}\sim10^{-3}Z_\odot\).

### Typical simulation setup
The classic three-dimensional simulations followed the collapse of a primordial protogalactic cloud or minihalo, usually with:

- total mass of order \(10^6\,M_\odot\) at redshift \(z\sim20\)–30;
- dark matter, gas rotation, and self-gravity;
- nonequilibrium primordial chemistry and \(\mathrm{H_2}\) cooling;
- an imposed, spatially uniform metallicity, commonly \(Z=0,\ 10^{-4},\ 10^{-3},\) and \(10^{-2}Z_\odot\);
- cooling from metal fine-structure lines, especially C II and O I;
- sink particles or bound clumps used to represent collapsing protostellar objects.

### Key findings
- **Below roughly \(10^{-4}Z_\odot\):** metal cooling is too weak to change the primordial thermal evolution. The gas remains relatively warm, around a few hundred kelvin, and fragments into large clumps associated with massive Population III stars.
- **At \(Z\gtrsim10^{-3.5}\)–\(10^{-3}Z_\odot\):** C and O fine-structure cooling lets the gas cool rapidly, often toward the cosmic microwave background temperature floor. The Jeans mass falls, and the cloud breaks into many smaller fragments—marking the onset of lower-mass, second-generation Population II star formation.
- The transition is not perfectly sharp and depends on density, abundance pattern, radiation background, and numerical resolution.

An important qualification is that simulations including **dust cooling at much higher densities** can produce low-mass fragments at metallicities as low as \(10^{-6}\)–\(10^{-5}Z_\odot\). Thus \(10^{-3.5}Z_\odot\) is mainly the critical metallicity for the **metal-line-cooling pathway**, while dust provides a lower-metallicity route to low-mass star formation.
counterfactuals.label: cf_3

counterfactuals.prompt: Describe how metal-line cooling affects fragmentation in a 5 × 10^5 solar-mass dark matter halo at redshift z ≈ 18, comparing simulations with Z = 0, 10^-4, 10^-3, and 10^-2 Zsolar.
counterfactuals.output:
Metal-line cooling introduces a sharp transition in the collapse behavior of a \(5\times10^{5}\,M_\odot\) minihalo at \(z\simeq18\). At this redshift, the CMB imposes a temperature floor of about \(T_{\rm CMB}\simeq52\) K.

| Metallicity | Thermal evolution and fragmentation |
|---|---|
| \(Z=0\) | Cooling is dominated by \(\mathrm{H_2}\). The gas stalls near \(T\sim200\) K, collapses into one main central concentration, and shows little cloud-scale fragmentation. The corresponding Jeans mass remains relatively large. |
| \(10^{-4}\,Z_\odot\) | Fine-structure cooling from species such as C II and O I is too weak to change the evolution substantially. Temperatures and morphology remain close to the primordial case, with little additional fragmentation. |
| \(10^{-3}\,Z_\odot\) | Metal-line cooling becomes dynamically important. The gas cools well below the \(\mathrm{H_2}\) floor, approaches the CMB temperature, and develops filaments and several gravitationally bound condensations. This marks the onset of efficient metal-induced fragmentation. |
| \(10^{-2}\,Z_\odot\) | Cooling is stronger and begins at lower density, producing colder, more structured gas and vigorous fragmentation into multiple clumps. However, once the gas reaches the CMB floor, extra metallicity cannot lower the temperature further, so fragment masses do not decrease indefinitely. |

Thus, these simulations imply a critical metallicity between roughly \(10^{-4}\) and \(10^{-3}\,Z_\odot\) for fragmentation driven by atomic metal lines. Above that threshold, cooling lowers the Jeans mass and converts the nearly monolithic primordial collapse into a clustered, multi-clump mode. This conclusion concerns metal-line cooling; dust cooling at much higher densities can introduce additional fragmentation not captured by this comparison.
counterfactuals.label: cf_4

counterfactuals.prompt: Generate a concise astrophysics research summary about simulations beginning at z = 99 that show a sharp change in stellar fragmentation near a critical metallicity of 10^-3 Zsolar.
counterfactuals.output: Cosmological simulations initialized at redshift \(z=99\) reveal a sharp transition in star-forming cloud fragmentation near a critical metallicity of \(Z_{\rm crit}\sim10^{-3}\,Z_\odot\). Below this threshold, inefficient metal cooling keeps collapsing gas relatively warm, favoring limited fragmentation and massive stellar clumps. At or above \(Z_{\rm crit}\), metal-line and dust-assisted cooling lower the gas temperature, reduce the Jeans mass, and produce many compact, low-mass fragments. The results support a rapid shift from Population III–like star formation toward a more conventional stellar initial mass distribution once early chemical enrichment reaches roughly one-thousandth of the solar metallicity.
counterfactuals.label: cf_5
